title: Rêveries du promeneur solitaire
author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
blurb: An old man walks alone around Paris and thinks: a dog that knocks him down and the strange joy of waking, a boat drifting on a Swiss lake, a factory hidden in a ravine, and thirty sous of wafers.

p: Here I am, then, alone on earth, with no brother, no friend, no company left but myself.
The most sociable and most loving of men has been driven out from everywhere, by unanimous agreement.
For years, I struggled against this injustice. I wanted to defend myself, explain myself, convince people. I only managed to wear myself out.
Today, I have stopped fighting. Since people did not want me, I shall do without them.
I still have a few years left to live, and I want to devote them to knowing myself.
Every day, I take a long walk, alone, in the countryside around Paris, and I let my mind go where it likes.
In the evening, I shall write down what I thought. These pages will be read by nobody but me. They will be the diary of my reveries.
On Thursday 24 October 1776, after dinner I followed the boulevards as far as the rue du Chemin-Vert, and I climbed up to the heights of Ménilmontant.
From there, I took paths through the vineyards and the meadows. I was looking for plants, and I found two that I had never seen around Paris.
The countryside, still green but already almost deserted, offered a picture of solitude and of approaching winter. It reminded me of my own old age.
Around six o'clock, I was coming back down towards the city, when the people walking in front of me suddenly stepped aside.
I saw a big Great Dane running at full speed ahead of a carriage, and rushing straight at me.
I did not have time to step aside. The dog hit me at full tilt, and I fell head first onto the cobblestones.
When I came round, it was almost dark. Three or four young men were holding me in their arms and telling me what had just happened to me.
That moment was delightful. I felt nothing but the present moment. I remembered nothing; I knew neither who I was nor where I was.
I saw the sky, a few stars, a little greenery. It seemed to me that I was being born into life, and that I was filling with my slight existence all the things I could see.
I watched my blood flow as I would have watched a stream flow, without thinking that the blood belonged to me.
I felt no pain, no fear, no worry. I have never felt anything comparable in any of the pleasures I have known.
Of all the places I have lived, none made me so truly happy as the island of Saint-Pierre, in the middle of Lake Biel, in Switzerland.
I stayed there only two months, in 1765, but I would have spent two years there, two centuries and all eternity without being bored for a moment.
This little island has only one house, large and comfortable, where the steward and his family lived.
Around it, there are fields, vineyards, woods, meadows, and banks covered with trees.
The shores of Lake Biel are wilder and more romantic than those of Lake Geneva, because the rocks and the woods come closer to the water there.
There are few roads, few travellers, and nothing disturbs the silence but the cry of the birds and the sound of the torrents falling from the mountain.
I had decided to do nothing. My books and papers stayed shut in their crates; instead of writing, I spent my mornings studying the island's plants.
I wanted to describe all those that grew there, without leaving out a single one, and I went from one spot to another, magnifying glass in hand, like a child at play.
One day, I even took everyone over to the little neighbouring island, to settle a family of rabbits there. We were as proud as the Argonauts.
After dinner, while the others were still at table, I would slip away and go and throw myself into a boat, alone.
I rowed out to the middle of the lake, when the water was calm, and there I stretched out full length in the boat, my eyes turned to the sky.
I let myself go and drift slowly wherever the water took me, sometimes for several hours.
I was plunged into a thousand vague but delightful reveries, which had no definite object, and which I nevertheless preferred to everything the world calls pleasures.
In the evening, I would go down to the edge of the lake, and sit on the sand, in some hidden spot.
There, the sound of the waves and the movement of the water, by holding my senses, drove every other agitation from my soul, and plunged it into a delightful reverie.
The ebb and flow of the water, its continuous but gentle sound, were enough to make me feel my existence with pleasure, without taking the trouble to think.
Often, night would take me by surprise there, and someone would have to come and fetch me.
Thinking back on that time, I wonder what made it so happy. It was not moments of rapture or passion: those are rare and quick.
Everything on earth is in continual flux. Nothing there keeps a constant form, and our affections, which attach themselves to external things, pass and change as they do.
Always ahead of us or behind us, they recall the past, which is no more, or announce the future, which often is never to be.
In our keenest enjoyments there is hardly a single moment when the heart can say to us: 'I wish this moment would last for ever.'
But if there is a state in which the soul finds a resting place solid enough to settle there entirely, without needing to recall the past or think of the future;
where time counts for nothing, where the present lasts for ever, with no feeling other than that of our existence;
as long as that state lasts, the person who is in it can call himself happy.
What does one enjoy in such a situation? Nothing outside oneself, nothing but oneself and one's own existence.
As long as that state lasts, one is sufficient unto oneself, like God.
That is the state I often found myself in on the island of Saint-Pierre, lying in my boat or sitting at the water's edge.

book.fr: Le petit garçon de la barrière
book.en: The little boy at the gate
p: There is, at the corner of the boulevard, at the exit of the Enfer toll gate, a place I often passed during my walks.
A woman sold fruit and bread there, and she had a very sweet little boy, but lame, who walked on crutches.
He would come up to passers-by to ask them for alms, with great charm.
I got to know this little fellow. Each time, he would come and pay me his little compliment, always followed by his little request, and I gave him a few sous with pleasure.
For some time, it was a real happiness for me to see him.
But little by little, this pleasure became a habit, then the habit became a kind of duty, and I ended up feeling this duty as a burden.
I then got into the habit of making a detour, so as not to go past that spot.
This little story made me think. I know that there is no true good without pleasure, and that I like to do good when my heart desires it.
But as soon as a good deed becomes an obligation, it loses all its charm for me.
I am not proud of it. But I prefer to tell the truth about myself rather than make myself out to be more virtuous than I am.
At my age, I have found a child's passion again: botany.
I set out in the morning with my magnifying glass and my book, and I spend hours looking at a flower, its petals, its stamens, its pistil.
Plants ask nothing of me. They do not judge me, they do not deceive me, and they are so beautiful that they make me forget people.
Other people look in plants for remedies or food. I look in them only for the pleasure of knowing them.
I remember a walk in the mountains of Switzerland, many years ago.
Following the plants, I had gone down into a ravine so deep and so wild that I believed myself the first man ever to have set foot there.
I sat down on the moss, between rocks and fir trees, and I began to dream, as proud as an explorer discovering a desert island.
Suddenly, I heard a small, regular noise, which I thought I recognised.
I got up, slipped through the undergrowth, and discovered, twenty steps away from me, a stocking factory.
My first reaction was anger: even here, people had come before me!
Then I began to laugh at myself. Only in Switzerland, I thought, can you find a factory at the bottom of a precipice.
One summer's day, I was walking in the Bois de Boulogne, near the Château de la Muette.
About twenty little girls were playing there, watched over by a nun.
A wafer seller came by with his drum and his lottery wheel: for a sou, you spun the wheel, and you won one, two or three wafers.
I could clearly see that the little girls wanted some very much, but that most of them had no money.
I called the seller over, and I told him to let all the little girls have a turn each, at my expense.
These words produced in the whole group a joy so lively that it alone would have been enough to repay everything I had in my purse.
So that there would be no jealousy, I arranged for those who won to share with the others, and everyone was happy.
This little party cost me thirty sous, but it made me happier than many far bigger expenses.
On my way home that evening, I understood something I had long forgotten.
The greatest pleasure I know is not being loved, nor admired; it is seeing happy faces, and knowing that I have had something to do with it.
